text:
Running the real tui shell confirmed the pure-Rust stack renders (real C-ABI `nmp_app_open_feed` + `compose_chirp_runtime` + `Difference(follows,mute)` + `decode_op_feed_snapshot` all surface the notes). So the break is host-side — and I found it: BOTH the generated iOS `ProjectionCache.generated.swift:177` and the Android `ProjectionCache.kt:194` (the NMP-owned rev-aware host apply caches) skip a `Changed` row when `incomingRev <= cached.rev`. App-owned keys like `chirp.timeline.home` emit `projection_rev = 0` on EVERY tick (they're absent from the kernel's builtin rev manifest — `rung2_stamp.rs:31-33`). So the host commits the FIRST (empty) home-feed frame at rev 0, then skips every later card-bearing frame (`0 <= 0`) → frozen empty while the envelope rev (your "decodedRev") climbs to 26. That is exactly "decodedRev advanced to 26 yet no card." [...] 2. EMISSION LADDER — NO REGRESSION, strictly better. Rung 3 (kernel/update/rung3_omit.rs:63-70) decides omission from MANIFEST PRESENCE, never from entry.projection_rev; keys absent from the manifest default to Changed and are "always kept, never omitted (D3-7)". App-owned keys can never enter the manifest (build_manifest at projection_rev/mod.rs:392 enumerates exactly KERNEL_BUILTIN_PROJECTION_KEYS, test-enforced by build_manifest_covers_all_builtin_keys). So wire emission counts for app-owned keys are byte-for-byte unchanged; the only behavioral delta is host-side: unchanged payloads now keep their prior rev so rev-aware hosts correctly skip re-decode (an improvement — before the bug, they wrongly skipped everything; the naive alternative would wastefully re-decode every tick since app-owned rows are emitted every tick).

3. OTHER CONSUMERS — none affected. The only rev-GATING consumers in the tree are the generated Swift/Kotlin ProjectionCaches (nmp-codegen/src/swift_projection_cache.rs, kotlin_projection_cache) — the exact caches this fixes. The web runtime and gallery only touch projectionRev in generated FlatBuffers decode accessors (no gating). The keyed caches (refs.profile/refs.event) ride the manifest path — Tier-2, untouched. No code anywhere treats rev==0 as a sentinel (grep clean; hits are FlatBuffers defaults). projection_emission.rs's emit_rev is a separate frame-level counter, unrelated. [...] `ProjectionRevTracker::stamp_app_owned_revs`: for app-owned (non-manifest) keys, derive a content-driven rev — a per-key counter that increments when the payload fingerprint changes — so the rev advances iff content changed. Cleared rows keep 0; Tier-2 built-ins untouched. Now `chirp.timeline.home` emits rev 1 (empty) → rev 2 (cards), so the host guard `2 <= 1` is false → it decodes the card frame → renders. Fixes iOS + Android + web at once (no per-platform host patch needed). [...] 4. FINGERPRINT MECHANISM — sound. DefaultHasher over payload bytes is deterministic in-process; per-key (u64 rev, u64 fp) slots in a HashMap keyed by projection key — correctly scoped, no cross-key sharing (test-covered). Kernel is a single-threaded actor with &mut self, so no concurrency hazard. Monotonic for the kernel's lifetime: the tracker is created once (kernel_new.rs:235) and app_owned_revs is never reset (reset_last_emitted doesn't touch it — correct). The `rev == 0 || last_fp != fp` bump means a Changed row never carries rev 0, and A→B→A content toggles keep advancing (1,2,3). The Cleared→Changed edge is safe: Cleared rows skip the slot (keep rev 0 on the wire), and the host cache REMOVES the entry on Cleared (swift_projection_cache.rs:236-238 doc: "Cleared row → remove from cache"), so a subsequent Changed at an unchanged rev is admitted (cache[key] is nil). Epoch/session change: host caches do a mandatory reset (D4, swift_projection_cache.rs:224) while kernel revs persist — safe in both directions. Residual risks are negligible: a 64-bit hash collision between consecutive distinct payloads would delay one frame until the next change (~2^-64, same risk class as every fingerprint gate already in this file, e.g. diagnostics_payload_fingerprint); the map never prunes Cleared keys (tiny tuples, bounded by distinct feed keys opened per session — and keeping them is the monotonicity-safe choice if a host ever misses a Cleared).
